newsitem.title: UK: LIFFE says CME link will boost Euromark volume.
newsitem.headline: LIFFE says CME link will boost Euromark volume.

text.p: The London International Financial Futures and Options Exchange's link up with the Chicago Mercantile Exchange (CME) will boost volume in the short-term mark interest rate futures and options contracts, LIFFE's chairman said on Wednesday.

"This move will significantly increase volume," Jack Wigglesworth, chairman of LIFFE told Reuters. "Our members want this. There is strong D-mark cash business in north America and we will see deepening liquidity."
Earlier, LIFFE announced it has reached an agreement with the CME to allow LIFFE's short-term interest rate futures and options to be traded on after the end of LIFFE's trading day.
LIFFE said the move was crucial to the exchange's strategy for European Economic and Monetary Union.
The Euromark interest rate future will be the first contract to start trading under the new arrangement.

"The Euromark is the most liquid short-term interest rate future in Europe and will settle against euros if EMU goes ahead. The link strengthens the contract and will distribute this benchmark instrument in the American time zone," said Wigglesworth.
He said no start date had been set, although the technical developments already underway in LIFFE's link up with the Chicago Board of Trade would faciliate the new project.
Wigglesworth said LIFFE had no plans to extend further its links with the CME at the long end of the yield curve, as the CBOT project would provide LIFFE with sufficient access to the U.S. time zone.

On Tuesday, the CBOT and LIFFE exchanges announced that the new tie-up would be amended to include trading long-dated euro debt products in its open outcry pits. After an initial postponement as a result of technical difficulties, the CBOT link is scheduled to go ahead on May 9, 1997.
French futures and options exchange MATIF also signed an accord on Wednesday with the CME which begins with the Matif's French bond future and will apply to all contracts of one year or more.

While the 10-year French franc bond future and options contracts will be the first to trade, the statement said the agreement applied to MATIF products with "a maturity of more than one year, denominated in francs, Ecu, the euro, or any other European currency."

Wigglesworth said LIFFE was in constant contact with other exchanges around the world, although he said it was not easy to establish joint-ventures with those in the same time zone without splitting liquidity.
He also said that that exchanges are aware of the threat posed to their positions if EMU goes ahead at the planned start date of January 1999.

"Under an EMU scenario there is the potential for very dramatic changes, institutional changes," said Wigglesworth. "Some exchanges, such as those that trade their own fixed income contracts only will cease to have a raison d'etre."
